meta.title: Who really said "Stand for something or you will fall for anything. Today's mighty oak is yesterday's nut that held its ground"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Two borrowed sayings welded together, neither traced to Rosa Parks. Quote Investigator dates the first to a 1945 journal article; the second is unsourced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Stand for something or you will fall for anything. Today's mighty oak is yesterday's nut that held its ground'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it as unsourced for Parks. QI's earliest close match for the first sentence: Gordon A. Eadie, Mental Hygiene, January 1945.

answer.label: Not Rosa Parks — two borrowed sayings welded together
answer.authorDates: Credited to Rosa Parks (1913–2005) · unsourced in her books, interviews and papers
answer.sourceLine: This is two sayings joined end to end, and neither belongs to Rosa Parks. The first is an anonymous modern proverb: Quote Investigator ↗ finds a precursor in a 1926 Iowa church announcement and its earliest close match in a January 1945 article by the physician Gordon A. Eadie, and its survey of who gets credit — Alexander Hamilton, Eadie, Irene Dunne, Peter Marshall and others — does not mention Parks. The second sentence is generally printed as David Icke’s, in the slightly different form “Today’s mighty oak is just yesterday’s nut, that held its ground”, and we could find no book, article or broadcast behind it.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — neither half has been traced to Parks, and the two sentences come from different places.

source.heading: Where the two sentences actually come from

docMeta.dd: Gordon A. Eadie, M.D. — though Quote Investigator notes it is unclear he coined it
Circulates as David Icke’s; no primary source located

source.excerpt: We are trying to show him not only what we are fighting against, but what we are fighting for. So many of these boys have only a very hazy idea of the real issues of the war. About all they see is “going back to the good old days.” This is a dangerous state. If they don’t stand for something, they will fall for anything.
trail: 1926–1927 — the earliest precursor on record is a Methodist church announcement in an Iowa newspaper; the next year an Ohio paper printed it as a “Sermonogram”: “It is easier to fall for anything than to stand for something” (Quote Investigator ↗).

January 1945 — the earliest close match appears in Dr Gordon A. Eadie’s article in Mental Hygiene. Yale University Press’s Dictionary of Modern Proverbs points to the same article and year for its earliest citation (Quote Investigator ↗).

May–July 1945 — the actress Irene Dunne ↗ spoke a version on the radio programme Town Meeting of the Air, and Reader’s Digest reprinted it that July crediting her — the step that carried the saying into wide circulation (Quote Investigator ↗).
The Parks attribution — the welded two-sentence version appears on Wikiquote only in the Unsourced list of its Talk:Rosa Parks ↗ page, not in any sourced section of her Wikiquote entry ↗.
source.excerptNote: Gordon A. Eadie, writing about returning war veterans in Mental Hygiene, January 1945 — the earliest close match Quote Investigator ↗ has found for the first sentence. Note the form: a description of “these boys”, not the imperative “Stand for something…” that circulates today.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted here. The first sentence is an anonymous modern proverb with no identified author; the second has no located source at all. The 1945 Mental Hygiene article carrying the earliest close match is itself a 1945 publication and so not in the public domain in the United States — but it is evidence about the proverb’s history, not a record of anything Rosa Parks said.

author.name: Rosa Parks
author.heading: About Rosa Parks
author.metaLine: 1913–2005 · Civil rights organiser, seamstress and NAACP secretary
author.bio: Rosa Parks was a trained organiser and secretary of the Montgomery NAACP long before her arrest on 1 December 1955 made her a national figure. She wrote and spoke carefully and at length — a memoir, an autobiography for young readers, decades of interviews, and the papers now held by the Library of Congress — which is exactly why an undocumented aphorism sits so oddly under her name. The words below are real; this one is not among them.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Gordon A. Eadie, M.D., “The Over-All Mental-Health Needs of the Industrial Plant, with Special Reference to War Veterans,” Mental Hygiene 29, no. 1 (January 1945): 103 — the earliest close match to the first sentence only, per Quote Investigator. The second sentence has no located source, and neither sentence is documented to Rosa Parks.

misattribution.heading: Two sayings, one famous name
misattribution.intro: Almost every quote site prints these two sentences together as a single Rosa Parks quotation. They are not one saying, they are two — with separate histories, neither of them hers.

items.why: It appears in none of her books or documented interviews. Wikiquote holds it only in the Unsourced list on its talk page ↗.
His Mental Hygiene article carries the earliest close match Quote Investigator ↗ has located, though QI notes it is not clear he coined it.
She spoke a version on radio in May 1945 and Reader’s Digest reprinted it that July under her name (Quote Investigator ↗).
A confusion with Alex Hamilton, a British broadcaster who used the saying in 1978 — more than a century and a half after the American statesman died (Quote Investigator ↗).

Quote sites credit him almost universally, usually in the form “Today’s mighty oak is just yesterday’s nut, that held its ground”. We could not locate a book, article or broadcast behind it, and Quote Investigator ↗ has no article on this sentence at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: the first sentence is an anonymous modern proverb from the mid-1940s, the second has no established origin, and Rosa Parks ↗ said neither.

context.heading: Why this one sticks to her
lead: Parks is a magnet for this kind of line because the sentiment fits the story everyone knows — a woman who would not move. Welding an inspirational proverb to a pun about acorns produces something that sounds like a civil-rights aphorism without being one.
What she actually said on the subject was plainer and better. Her own account of the arrest is a few flat sentences with no slogan in them at all.
detailsBody: The two halves can be pulled apart cleanly. The “stand for something” proverb has a documented mid-century trail through a medical journal, a radio broadcast and Reader’s Digest, and picked up a series of false attributions along the way — Alexander Hamilton, Peter Marshall, and eventually Parks.

The “mighty oak” sentence behaves differently: it has no paper trail at all, only a dense layer of quote-aggregator pages crediting David Icke without a citation between them. Joined together and put under a famous name, two unsourced sentences read as one authoritative quotation.
context.pull: It sounds like her. That is the whole reason it travels.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest close match to "If they don’t stand for something, they will fall for anything" is Gordon A. Eadie in Mental Hygiene, January 1945, p. 103; a 1926 Iowa church announcement is the earliest precursor; Irene Dunne and Reader’s Digest popularised it in 1945; QI concludes it is an anonymous modern proverb and never mentions Rosa Parks.
The welded two-sentence version is listed under "Unsourced" on Wikiquote’s Rosa Parks talk page.
Wikiquote’s sourced Rosa Parks entry does not contain this two-sentence saying.
Quote Investigator has no article on "Today’s mighty oak is yesterday’s nut that held its ground" — a site search returns no results.
David Icke is a British former footballer and broadcaster turned conspiracy theorist.
Irene Dunne was an American film actress active in the 1930s and 1940s.
